title: Security & Networking
description: A learning path from network basics and communication through identity, cryptography, system security, OT security, and governance. Use the domain filter to focus a topic and follow 'understand before' edges to find prerequisites.

nodes.label: Networking Fundamentals
nodes.description: How devices identify each other and move data across local and distant networks. Start here before protocols, access controls, or OT segmentation.

nodes.label: Network Services & Protocols
nodes.description: Rules and services that let applications find peers, establish connections, and exchange data.

nodes.label: Identity & Access Management
nodes.description: How people and services are represented and managed across systems.

nodes.label: Authentication & Authorization
nodes.description: How a system verifies who is calling, decides what they may do, and delegates access.

nodes.label: Cryptography & PKI
nodes.description: Keys, encryption, hashes, signatures, and certificates used to protect data and establish trust.

nodes.label: Application & API Security
nodes.description: Controls that protect web applications and APIs from unsafe input, browser attacks, and exposed secrets.

nodes.label: Network Security
nodes.description: Controls for limiting, inspecting, and securing communication between network zones.

nodes.label: Infrastructure & Endpoint Security
nodes.description: Protecting operating systems and hosts through maintenance, configuration, and vulnerability reduction.

nodes.label: Resilience & Availability
nodes.description: Engineering systems to keep working or recover after faults and incidents. These are reliability concepts as well as security concerns.

nodes.label: Security Operations
nodes.description: Collecting evidence, finding problems, responding to incidents, and reducing known weaknesses.

nodes.label: OT & ICS Security
nodes.description: Applying security to industrial control while accounting for process safety, availability, and long equipment lifecycles.

nodes.label: Governance, Risk & Compliance
nodes.description: How organizations decide what to protect, evaluate risk, and meet policy, standard, and legal duties.

nodes.label: Threats & Attack Techniques
nodes.description: Potential harmful actions and the ways attackers try to reach systems and data.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.description: Connected devices that can exchange data over a shared medium or routed links. Boundaries and paths determine which devices can communicate.

nodes.label: LAN
nodes.description: Local area network within a limited site, such as a plant or office. A LAN can contain multiple IP subnets and VLANs.

nodes.label: WAN
nodes.description: Wide area network linking separate sites or regions. WAN links commonly carry traffic between LANs through routers.

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.description: Common local network technology that carries frames using MAC addresses. IP traffic often runs over Ethernet, but Ethernet itself is not IP.

nodes.label: MAC Address
nodes.description: Link-layer address used to deliver Ethernet frames on a local network. Switches learn MAC locations; routers use IP addresses to route between networks.

nodes.label: IP Address
nodes.description: Logical address identifying a network interface for IP communication. Its network portion and route determine where packets can be delivered.

nodes.label: IPv4
nodes.description: Version of IP with 32-bit addresses, often written as four decimal numbers. Private IPv4 addresses commonly need NAT for internet access.

nodes.label: IPv6
nodes.description: Version of IP with 128-bit addresses and a much larger address space. IPv6 routing still depends on prefixes and gateways.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.description: A range of IP addresses sharing a network prefix. A subnet defines which destinations are local; a VLAN instead separates link-layer traffic.

nodes.label: CIDR
nodes.description: Prefix notation such as 192.0.2.0/24 that states how many leading address bits identify a network. It describes subnet size and routing prefixes.

nodes.label: Default Gateway
nodes.description: Router address a host sends packets to when the destination is outside its local subnet. It is not the Ignition Gateway service.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.description: Choosing a next hop for IP packets between networks. Routers use routes and destination prefixes rather than Ethernet MAC addresses alone.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.description: Device that forwards IP packets between networks using routing decisions. A switch normally forwards local frames using MAC addresses.

nodes.label: Switch
nodes.description: Device that forwards Ethernet frames within a link-layer network using learned MAC addresses. Some switches also provide Layer 3 routing.

nodes.label: OSI Model
nodes.description: Seven-layer reference model for reasoning about communication problems. Ethernet, IP, and TCP are often explained using its link, network, and transport layers.

nodes.label: ARP
nodes.description: On IPv4 local networks, resolves a neighbor's IP address to its MAC address so an Ethernet frame can reach it. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.

nodes.label: VLAN
nodes.description: Logical separation of Ethernet traffic into Layer 2 broadcast domains. A VLAN often maps to an IP subnet but does not itself define one or enforce a firewall policy.

nodes.label: NAT
nodes.description: Translates IP addresses at a network boundary; common internet access also translates ports (PAT). Translation alone is not a security policy.

nodes.label: Private IP Address
nodes.description: Address from ranges reserved for private IPv4 networks and not globally routed on the internet. It can reach external services through NAT or a proxy.

nodes.label: Public IP Address
nodes.description: Globally routable IP address used for internet reachability, subject to routing and firewall policy. Having one does not mean every port is reachable.

nodes.label: Domain Name
nodes.description: Human-readable name such as example.com. DNS records can map it to addresses and other service information.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Distributed naming service that resolves domain names to IP addresses and other records. It helps clients find servers without hard-coding addresses.

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.description: Automatically leases IP configuration such as address, subnet prefix, gateway, and DNS server to a host. It does not resolve names; DNS does that.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.description: Connection-oriented transport with ordered, reliable byte delivery. Its handshake establishes a connection before application data is exchanged.

nodes.label: UDP
nodes.description: Connectionless transport that sends datagrams without TCP's built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. Applications may add reliability when needed.

nodes.label: Port
nodes.description: Number that identifies a transport endpoint on a host, interpreted with IP address and protocol. Firewalls commonly filter by ports, but a port is not a service identity.

nodes.label: Socket
nodes.description: Operating-system endpoint an application uses for network communication. A TCP connection identifies both ends by address and port.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.description: Application protocol for requests and responses used by web pages and APIs. Plain HTTP provides no transport encryption by itself.

nodes.label: HTTPS
nodes.description: HTTP carried over TLS to protect traffic and authenticate the server when certificates are validated. It does not make unsafe application logic safe.

nodes.label: TLS
nodes.description: Protocol that negotiates encrypted, integrity-protected communication and usually authenticates the server using certificates. A certificate supplies identity and key material; it is not TLS itself.

nodes.label: SSH
nodes.description: Encrypted protocol for remote shell access and related services. It authenticates the remote host and can authenticate users with keys or passwords.

nodes.label: MQTT
nodes.description: Publish/subscribe messaging protocol often used for telemetry. Use TLS, client authentication, and broker permissions when crossing trust boundaries.

nodes.label: OPC UA
nodes.description: Industrial interoperability protocol and information model used by SCADA and devices. Its security modes can authenticate peers and protect messages.

nodes.label: REST API
nodes.description: HTTP API organized around resources and standard request methods. Authentication, authorization, validation, and TLS still have to be designed.

nodes.label: Proxy
nodes.description: Forward proxy makes requests on behalf of clients, often controlling outbound access. A reverse proxy instead accepts inbound requests on behalf of servers.

nodes.label: Reverse Proxy
nodes.description: Front end for one or more servers that receives client requests and routes them to backends. It can terminate TLS, but backend access control still matters.

nodes.label: Identity
nodes.description: Representation of a person, device, or service recognized by a system. An identity answers who or what an entity is; permissions are separate.

nodes.label: User
nodes.description: Human principal with an account or federated identity. Applications link actions and permissions to the user identity.

nodes.label: Service Account
nodes.description: Non-human account used by software to call another service. It needs scoped permissions and managed credentials rather than a shared human login.

nodes.label: IAM
nodes.description: Identity and access management: lifecycle, authentication, roles, and permissions for users and services. It makes access decisions manageable across systems.

nodes.label: Identity Provider (IdP)
nodes.description: Service that authenticates users and provides identity assertions or tokens to applications. The relying application still decides what the user may do.

nodes.label: Directory Service
nodes.description: Stores and organizes identities, groups, and related attributes for lookup and administration. It is not automatically the same thing as an IdP.

nodes.label: Active Directory
nodes.description: Microsoft on-premises directory and domain services for users, computers, and policies. It often backs enterprise authentication and authorization.

nodes.label: Authentication
nodes.description: Verifies a claimed identity using a credential or other evidence. It answers who is calling; authorization decides what that identity may do.

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.description: Checks whether an authenticated principal may perform a specific action on a resource. It must be enforced even when login succeeded.

nodes.label: MFA
nodes.description: Requires evidence from more than one factor to strengthen authentication. It reduces harm from a stolen password but does not replace authorization.

nodes.label: Role
nodes.description: Named grouping of permissions assigned to principals. Roles simplify access reviews when they reflect actual job needs.

nodes.label: RBAC
nodes.description: Role-based access control grants permissions through assigned roles. It differs from attribute-based rules that evaluate context and properties.

nodes.label: Least Privilege
nodes.description: Grant only the access needed for a task and remove it when no longer needed. This limits damage from mistakes or compromised accounts.

nodes.label: SSO
nodes.description: Single sign-on lets a user access multiple applications through one authentication relationship. Each application must still enforce its own permissions.

nodes.label: Credentials
nodes.description: Secrets or other proof used to authenticate a principal, such as passwords or private-key possession. Tokens usually represent granted access after authentication, not the user's password.

nodes.label: API Key
nodes.description: Application-issued string identifying or authenticating a calling client. Treat it as a secret and scope, rotate, and monitor it where supported.

nodes.label: Access Token
nodes.description: Credential a client presents to a resource server for scoped access. It may be opaque or use JWT format; possession alone is not proof of a human login.

nodes.label: Refresh Token
nodes.description: Credential used with an authorization server to request new access tokens. It is not sent to the resource API and needs especially careful storage.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0
nodes.description: Framework for delegated access to resources using scoped tokens. OAuth alone does not define a standard user-authentication protocol; OIDC adds that layer.

nodes.label: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
nodes.description: Identity layer built on OAuth 2.0 that lets clients verify a user's authentication and obtain identity claims. Its ID token is commonly a JWT.

nodes.label: JWT
nodes.description: Compact format for carrying claims, often signed. A JWT is a format, not an authentication mechanism or proof that a token is trustworthy without validation.

nodes.label: Encryption
nodes.description: Transforms plaintext into ciphertext using a key so unauthorized readers cannot recover it. Unlike hashing, authorized holders can decrypt it.

nodes.label: Symmetric Encryption
nodes.description: Encryption in which both sides use the same shared secret key. It is efficient for bulk data, but the key must be exchanged safely.

nodes.label: Asymmetric Cryptography
nodes.description: Cryptography using a related public and private key pair. It supports key exchange and signatures; bulk traffic is usually protected with symmetric keys.

nodes.label: Public Key
nodes.description: Shareable half of a key pair, used for tasks such as verifying signatures or establishing encrypted channels. It should be bound to the right identity.

nodes.label: Private Key
nodes.description: Secret half of an asymmetric key pair, used for signing or key agreement. Exposure can let an attacker impersonate its holder.

nodes.label: Cryptographic Key
nodes.description: Value controlling a cryptographic operation. A key may be symmetric, public, or private; it is not the same as a hash digest.

nodes.label: Secret
nodes.description: Value that must be kept confidential, such as a password, API key, or symmetric key. A public key and an ordinary hash digest are not secrets.

nodes.label: Cryptographic Hash
nodes.description: One-way function producing a fixed-size digest of data, used for integrity checks and as a building block in password storage and signatures. A hash does not encrypt data or require a secret key.

nodes.label: Salt
nodes.description: Unique, non-secret value mixed into each password before a password-hashing function. It prevents identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes.

nodes.label: HMAC
nodes.description: Combines a cryptographic hash with a secret key to authenticate message integrity. Unlike a plain hash, verification requires knowledge of the shared secret.

nodes.label: Digital Signature
nodes.description: Cryptographic proof made with a private key and checked with the corresponding public key. It supports integrity and signer authentication, not secrecy.

nodes.label: Certificate
nodes.description: Usually an X.509 document binding a subject identity to a public key, signed by an issuer. Validation includes the name, validity, and trust chain.

nodes.label: Certificate Authority (CA)
nodes.description: Issuer that signs certificates after applying identity and issuance checks. Trust depends on the CA chain and how it is configured on the client.

nodes.label: PKI
nodes.description: Public key infrastructure: policies, CAs, certificates, trust stores, and lifecycle processes for public-key trust. A certificate alone is only one part.

nodes.label: Input Validation
nodes.description: Checks incoming data against expected format and meaning before use. It reduces injection and logic errors, alongside safe APIs and output encoding.

nodes.label: CORS
nodes.description: Browser mechanism by which a server permits selected cross-origin script requests. It is not authentication and does not restrict non-browser clients or iframe embedding.

nodes.label: CSRF
nodes.description: Cross-site request forgery tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted action. Anti-CSRF tokens and suitable cookie settings help defend against it.

nodes.label: XSS
nodes.description: Cross-site scripting makes untrusted content run as script in a user's browser. Context-aware output encoding and safe DOM APIs reduce the risk.

nodes.label: SQL Injection
nodes.description: Untrusted input changes a database query's structure. Parameterized queries keep input as data instead of SQL instructions.

nodes.label: UUID / GUID
nodes.description: Identifier format for objects such as users or database records; GUID is a common Microsoft term. Uniqueness is not secrecy, authentication, or an access-control boundary.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.description: Enforces traffic rules between hosts or networks using attributes such as addresses, ports, and state. An ACL is a rule list often used by a firewall or router.

nodes.label: ACL
nodes.description: Access control list of permit or deny rules applied to a resource or network traffic. Its effectiveness depends on where and how the rules are enforced.

nodes.label: Network Segmentation
nodes.description: Divides a network into zones and controls paths between them. VLANs create logical separation; firewalls or equivalent controls enforce policy between zones.

nodes.label: DMZ
nodes.description: Intermediate network zone for systems exposed to less trusted networks. Controlled flows reduce direct access to protected internal networks.

nodes.label: Industrial DMZ
nodes.description: Controlled boundary between enterprise IT and OT networks for mediated data exchange and remote access. It is a design pattern, not an ISA-95 functional level.

nodes.label: IDS
nodes.description: Intrusion detection system that observes traffic or hosts and raises alerts about suspicious activity. Detection differs from an IPS that can actively block traffic.

nodes.label: VPN
nodes.description: Encrypts traffic between endpoints across another network. A VPN secures the path but does not by itself decide what a connected user may access.

nodes.label: Secure Remote Access
nodes.description: Controlled access to remote systems using identity checks, limited permissions, monitoring, and often a VPN or jump host. OT access should also respect operations and safety.

nodes.label: Zero Trust
nodes.description: Approach that verifies each access request using identity, device, and context rather than trusting location alone. It does not mean removing all network boundaries.

nodes.label: Operating System
nodes.description: Software managing a host's processes, files, accounts, and network interfaces. Windows and Linux servers need secure configuration and updates.

nodes.label: Patch Management
nodes.description: Tests and applies updates that fix defects and vulnerabilities. OT schedules may require compensating controls when equipment cannot be patched quickly.

nodes.label: Hardening
nodes.description: Reduces unnecessary services, privileges, and unsafe defaults on a host. It narrows the attack surface alongside patching and monitoring.

nodes.label: Vulnerability
nodes.description: Weakness that could be exploited under the right conditions. A published CVE identifies a known vulnerability but does not by itself quantify local risk.

nodes.label: Availability
nodes.description: Ability of a system or service to be usable when needed. It is part of the CIA triad and particularly important in production control and safety contexts.

nodes.label: Failover
nodes.description: Switches service to a standby component after a failure. It uses redundancy, but the switch may still take time or lose in-flight work.

nodes.label: Redundancy
nodes.description: Extra components or paths that reduce single points of failure. It enables failover but does not guarantee seamless high availability.

nodes.label: High Availability
nodes.description: Design goal of keeping service interruptions short through redundancy, monitoring, and failover. A backup supports later recovery but is not live availability.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.description: Separate copy of data or configuration that can be restored after loss or corruption. Test restoration; backups do not keep a running service online.

nodes.label: RPO
nodes.description: Recovery point objective: maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured as time since the last recoverable point. It guides backup frequency.

nodes.label: RTO
nodes.description: Recovery time objective: target time to restore service after an outage. It guides recovery procedures and capacity planning.

nodes.label: Logging
nodes.description: Records events that explain what a system did and who acted. Useful security logs need reliable timestamps, retention, and protection from tampering.

nodes.label: SIEM
nodes.description: Security information and event management collects and correlates logs for detection and investigation. It needs useful sources and response processes.

nodes.label: Incident Response
nodes.description: Coordinated detection, containment, analysis, recovery, and learning after a suspected security incident. Plans matter before an event occurs.

nodes.label: Vulnerability Management
nodes.description: Continuously identifies, prioritizes, and addresses weaknesses based on exposure and impact. It includes patching and compensating controls.

nodes.label: OT
nodes.description: Operational technology monitors or controls physical processes. Safety and availability constraints often change how security controls are deployed.

nodes.label: ICS
nodes.description: Industrial control systems combine control devices, networks, and supervision to run physical processes. They are a major part of OT.

nodes.label: SCADA
nodes.description: Supervisory control and data acquisition systems collect process data and provide operator supervision. They often communicate with PLCs and remote devices.

nodes.label: PLC
nodes.description: Programmable logic controller executes control logic close to equipment. Its communications and engineering access need protection without disrupting the process.

nodes.label: Purdue Model
nodes.description: Layered reference view of industrial system and network zones, often used in segmentation discussions. It is not itself a cybersecurity standard or a mandatory placement rule.

nodes.label: ISA-95
nodes.description: Standard for enterprise-to-control integration, manufacturing functions, and information exchange. Its levels help discuss OT architecture but are not security requirements.

nodes.label: ISA/IEC 62443
nodes.description: Industrial automation and control systems security standards covering lifecycle, organizational, system, and component requirements. Unlike ISA-95, this series is specifically about security.

nodes.label: Zones and Conduits
nodes.description: ISA/IEC 62443 approach grouping assets with similar security needs into zones and controlling communication through conduits. It makes trust boundaries explicit.

nodes.label: Governance
nodes.description: Defines accountability, policy, and oversight for security decisions. It helps turn technical controls into a managed program.

nodes.label: Risk
nodes.description: Potential loss when a threat can exploit a vulnerability and cause impact. Likelihood and impact inform prioritization; a vulnerability alone is not a risk score.

nodes.label: CIA Triad
nodes.description: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are three common security objectives. OT designs often give availability and process safety particular weight.

nodes.label: NIS2
nodes.description: EU directive requiring covered sectors to manage cybersecurity risk and report significant incidents through national implementing law. Applicability depends on organization and jurisdiction.

nodes.label: GDPR
nodes.description: EU framework for processing and protecting personal data. It addresses privacy and data protection, not all aspects of cybersecurity.

nodes.label: ISO/IEC 27001
nodes.description: Requirements for an information security management system that manages risk and continual improvement. Certification evaluates the management system, not immunity from attacks.

nodes.label: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
nodes.description: Outcome-based framework for managing cybersecurity risk through Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover functions. It is guidance, not a product checklist.

nodes.label: Threat
nodes.description: Potential cause of harm, including malicious actors, mistakes, or environmental events. Risk depends on what it could exploit and the resulting impact.

nodes.label: Phishing
nodes.description: Deceptive message or page intended to steal credentials or induce unsafe action. MFA helps, but users and systems still need other checks.

nodes.label: Ransomware
nodes.description: Malware that disrupts access to data or systems, often by encryption and extortion. Segmentation, limited privileges, and tested backups reduce impact.
